newsitem.title: USA: California legislature passes $68 billion budget.
newsitem.headline: California legislature passes $68 billion budget.

text.p: The California legislature Monday passed a $68 billion state budget, ending the second-longest budget deadlock in state history, while Gov. Pete Wilson signed a sweeping welfare reform law.

The state Assembly voted 58-15 to approve a budget compromise hammered out by Wilson and legislative leaders. A few hours earlier, the state Senate voted 30-6 for the bill, giving it the required two-thirds majority in both houses.

Each house still has to work its way through about 36 "trailer" bills implementing various parts of the budget package. Wilson, a Republican, has said he will not sign the budget until he gets all of the trailer bills.
The legislature passed the 1997/98 budget 42 days after the start of the fiscal year on July 1, a delay second only to 1992 when the state budget was passed 63 days late.
In 1992, the state was in the depths of a recession. This year's delay was more surprising because the California economy is growing strongly, boosting tax revenues.
The budget had been held up by months of wrangling between Republicans, led by Wilson, and Democrats who control the legislature.
One of the stumbling blocks was over welfare reform, a compromise version of which was finally passed by the legislature last week.
The far-reaching reform law, signed by Wilson Monday, sets strict time limits on how long people may receive aid and aims to move recipients from welfare to work.
Wilson said the new law would free "hundreds of thousands of men, women and children from a system of dependency that for too long has destroyed their hopes and stifled their ambition.
"From now on, welfare in California will be a temporary transition and it will be strictly time-limited," he added.

Wilson's office said the welfare reform bill, called the California Work Opportunity and Responsibility to Kids (CalWorks) plan, would "replace the state's failed welfare system with new rules based on work, accountability and personal responsibility."
The new law has been criticised by some Democrats who say it is too harsh on the poor.
The law contains a cumulative lifetime limit on aid of five years, including aid received from any other state before a recipient's move to California.

New applicants are eligible to receive assistance for 18 months at any one time, while current recipients are eligible for 24 months. Counties have the option of extending the 18-month deadline for up to six months.
If the recipient has not found a job when the time limit is reached, he or she enters community service employment.
